claim: Basement membranes (BMs) are cell-associated, dense, sheet-like forms of extracellular matrix that underlie all epithelia and endothelial tissue, and surround muscle, fat, and Schwann cells.
source: The basement membrane (BM) is a cell-associated, dense, sheet-like form of extracellular matrix that underlies all epithelia and endothelial tissue, and surrounds muscle, fat, and Schwann cells (Halfter et al., 2015; Yurchenco, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Halfter et al., 2015; Yurchenco, 2011).

claim: BMs are built on polymeric laminin and type IV collagen networks that arose at the time of animal multicellularity.
source: BMs are built on polymeric laminin and type IV collagen networks that arose at the time of animal multicellularity, and may have been required for the evolution of complex tissues (Hynes, 2012; Ozbek et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hynes, 2012; Ozbek et al., 2010).

claim: BMs provide tissues with mechanical support, barrier functions, and cues for polarization, differentiation and growth.
source: Consistent with this idea, BMs provide tissues with mechanical support, barrier functions, and cues for polarization, differentiation and growth (Breitkreutz et al., 2013; Hay, 1981; Poschl et al., 2004; Rasmussen et al., 2012; Suh and Miner, 2013; Yurchenco, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Live imaging studies have revealed that cell-BM interfaces are highly dynamic.
source: Although it was generally thought that cell-BM interactions are static, live imaging studies have revealed that cell-BM interfaces are highly dynamic (Morrissey and Sherwood, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Morrissey and Sherwood, 2015).

claim: During egg chamber rotation in Drosophila, follicle cells move along BM and deposit constricting strips of aligned type IV collagen, which direct egg elongation along the anterior-posterior axis.
source: Examples of cell-BM sliding are varied and include egg chamber rotation in Drosophila, where the follicle cells move along BM and deposit constricting strips of aligned type IV collagen, which direct egg elongation along the anterior-posterior axis (Cetera and Horne-Badovinac, 2015; Haigo and Bilder, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Cetera and Horne-Badovinac, 2015; Haigo and Bilder, 2011).

claim: During salivary gland growth in vertebrates, the BM slides away from the bud tip toward the duct, allowing bud expansion while restricting growth at the duct.
source: During salivary gland growth in vertebrates, the BM slides away from the bud tip toward the duct, allowing bud expansion while restricting growth at the duct (Harunaga et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Harunaga et al., 2014).

claim: Intestinal epithelial cells derived from the stem cell crypt slide along the BM towards the villus tips during differentiation to rapidly renew the gut epithelium.
source: Further, BM labeling and pulse chase experiments revealed that intestinal epithelial cells derived from the stem cell crypt slide along the BM towards the villus tips during differentiation to rapidly renew the gut epithelium (Clevers, 2013; Trier et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Clevers, 2013; Trier et al., 1990).

claim: During the mid-L3 larval stage, the uterine-vulval connection is initiated by the anchor cell (AC), which breaches the BM that separates the uterine and vulval tissues and attaches to the underlying vulval cells.
source: During the mid-L3 larval stage, the uterine-vulval connection is initiated by a specialized uterine cell, the anchor cell (AC), that breaches the BM that separate these tissues and attaches to the underlying vulval cells.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text describing the biological process.

claim: Following AC invasion, the gap in the BM widens further through BM sliding over the vulval and uterine cells, not through BM degradation.
source: BM gap widening does not involve BM degradation. Instead, optical highlighting of BM and manipulation of tissue dynamics has shown that growth and morphogenesis of the uterine and vulval tissues generate forces on the BM that drive BM sliding over the vulval and uterine cells to further expand the gap (Ihara et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Ihara et al., 2011) describing experimental evidence.

claim: The vulval E and F cells undergo precisely timed divisions to initiate BM sliding—cell rounding during divisions dramatically reduces cell contact with the BM and allows the BM to slide over the vulE and F cells.
source: The centrally located vulval E and F cells, which contact the BM gap boundary, undergo precisely timed divisions to initiate BM sliding--cell rounding during divisions dramatically reduces cell contact with the BM and allows the BM to slide over the vulE and F cells (Matus et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Matus et al., 2014).

claim: The BM stops sliding on the non-dividing vulD cell, which concentrates the BM adhesion receptor INA-1/PAT-3 (integrin) to stabilize the BM gap boundary.
source: The BM stops sliding on the non-dividing vulD cell, which concentrates the BM adhesion receptor INA-1/PAT-3 (integrin) to stabilize the BM gap boundary (Ihara et al., 2011; Matus et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ihara et al., 2011; Matus et al., 2014).

claim: The two most prominent classes of adhesion receptors that link BM to the cytoskeleton are integrin family members and the receptor dystroglycan.
source: Two of the most prominent classes of adhesion receptors that link BM to the cytoskeleton are integrin family members and the receptor dystroglycan (Bello et al., 2015; Kramer, 2005; Yurchenco, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bello et al., 2015; Kramer, 2005; Yurchenco, 2011).

claim: Through a mutagenesis screen, a putative null mutant in the gene encoding the LIN-29 protein was identified that is deficient in BM sliding.
source: Through this screen we identified a putative null mutant in the gene encoding the LIN-29 protein, which is a Kruppel-family EGR (early growth response) protein (Harris and Horvitz, 2011), that is deficient in BM sliding.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from a genetic screen described in the manuscript.

claim: LIN-29 is expressed and functions in the invading AC to promote BM sliding.
source: We show that LIN-29 is expressed and functions in the invading AC to promote BM sliding.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data including expression analysis and cell-specific rescue experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: LIN-29 regulates BM sliding through its role in maintaining AC expression of LAG-2, a transmembrane Notch ligand, which activates Notch signaling in the neighboring uterine π cells.
source: We further find that LIN-29 regulates BM sliding through its role in maintaining AC expression of LAG-2, a transmembrane Notch ligand, which activates Notch signaling in the neighboring BM gap boundary cells, the uterine π cells that sit on BM next to the nascent breach.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from RNAi experiments and genetic analysis described in the manuscript.

claim: Notch activation in uterine π cells upregulates ctg-1 expression, which encodes a Sec14-GOLD domain phosphatidylinositol transfer protein.
source: Through a targeted uterine-specific RNAi screen of putative direct Notch targets, we find that Notch activation in these uterine cells upregulates ctg-1 expression, which encodes a Sec14-GOLD domain phosphatidylinositol transfer protein that belongs to a class of proteins implicated in regulating vesicle trafficking (Grabon et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from an RNAi screen and expression analysis described in the manuscript.

claim: CTG-1 functions in the uterine π cells to limit the cell surface trafficking of DGN-1 (dystroglycan), and reduction of DGN-1 is sufficient to promote BM sliding.
source: Finally, using photobleaching, CRISPR/Cas-9 targeted knockout, and cell-specific rescue experiments, we demonstrate that CTG-1 functions in the uterine π cells to limit the cell surface trafficking of DGN-1 (dystroglycan), and that reduction of DGN-1 is sufficient to promote BM sliding.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from photobleaching, CRISPR/Cas-9 knockout, and rescue experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: The qy1 allele introduces a nonsense mutation near the start of the region encoding the DNA binding domain in all three known isoforms of lin-29.
source: We sequenced the qy1 allele and found that it introduces a nonsense mutation near the start of the region encoding the DNA binding domain in all three known isoforms of the gene (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on sequencing data and is illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The BM gap was significantly reduced in qy1 mutant animals compared to wild type.
source: The gap in the BM was significantly reduced in qy1 mutant animals (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: In wild type animals, the BM moved away from both the anterior and posterior sides of the AC in most animals (n = 13/20 animals), while in qy1 animals the BM never moved away from both sides of the AC (n = 0/20 animals).
source: Further, we found that that while in wild type animals, the BM moved away from both the anterior and posterior sides of the AC in most animals (n = 13/20 animals; the remaining 7 moved on one side), in qy1 animals the BM never moved away from both sides of the AC (n = 0/20 animals) and only occasionally moved slightly away from one side (n = 5/20 animals).
evidence: The claim is based on direct observation and quantification of BM movement in live animals.

claim: Optical highlighting experiments showed that marked edges of the BM gap moved away from the AC and rested over the vulD cell in wild type animals (n = 10/10 animals), but maintained contact with the AC in lin-29(qy1) mutants and failed to move over the vulD cell (n = 18/18 animals).
source: While marked edges of the BM gap moved away from the AC and rested over the vulD cell in wild type animals (n = 10/10 animals), optically highlighted segments maintained contact with the AC in lin-29(qy1) mutants and failed to move over the vulD cell (n = 18/18 animals; Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on photoconversion experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The morphology of the developing vulva—including the number of VPCs and their relative positions—was the same in lin-29(qy1) mutants compared with wild type animals.
source: Notably, the morphology of the developing vulva—including the number of VPCs and their relative positions (n = 15/15 animals, Figure 2B) and vulval height and width (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)—was the same in lin-29(qy1) mutants compared with wild type animals.
evidence: The claim is based on morphological analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: lin-29 is expressed in the AC throughout the course of uterine-vulval connection.
source: Using this reporter, we detected expression of lin-29 in the AC throughout the course of uterine-vulval connection (Figure 3A), but did not detect expression in the other cells in contact with or bordering the BM boundary.
evidence: The claim is based on expression analysis using a transcriptional reporter shown in Figure 3A.

claim: lin-29(ga94) mutants had a similar defect in the BM gap opening to qy1 mutants.
source: We measured BM gap expansion and found that ga94 mutants had a similar defect in the BM gap opening to qy1 mutants (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: AC-specific expression of LIN-29A::GFP completely rescued BM gap expansion in lin-29(qy1) mutant animals.
source: We found that LIN-29A::GFP protein expressed only in the AC completely rescued BM gap expansion (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: The claim is based on cell-specific rescue experiments shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: The BM gap still failed to open in the absence of the AC in lin-29 mutant animals (n = 8/8 animals).
source: We found that the BM gap still failed to open in the absence of the AC in lin-29 mutant animals (n = 8/8 animals, Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is based on laser ablation experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Ablation of the AC at the P6.p 4-cell stage in wild type animals does not prevent BM sliding and gap expansion.
source: Ablation of the AC at this stage in wild type animals does not prevent BM sliding and gap expansion (Ihara et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Ihara et al., 2011).

claim: The BM gap opened wider on the side of the AC in lin-29 mutants after laser ablation of the uterine π cells on that side (n = 5/8 animals).
source: However, the BM gap opened wider on the side of the AC in lin-29 mutants (BM slid over the vulD cell, outlined with dashed line) after laser ablation of the uterine π cells on that side (right, arrow, n = 5/8 animals; p<0.001, Fisher's Exact Test).
evidence: The claim is based on laser ablation experiments shown in Figure 4A with statistical analysis.

claim: Uterine-specific RNAi targeting lag-2 resulted in a BM sliding defect similar to lin-29 mutants.
source: Uterine lag-2 knockdown recapitulated the BM sliding defect seen in lin-29 mutants (Figure 4B,C), suggesting that the LIN-29 protein acts in a LAG-2 dependent manner to promote BM sliding.
evidence: The claim is based on RNAi experiments shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Loss of lin-12, but not glp-1, phenocopied lag-2 RNAi.
source: Consistent with LAG-2 acting through the LIN-12 (Notch) receptor, we also used RNAi targeting lin-12 and glp-1 (the only other encoded Notch receptor in the C. elegans genome) (Greenwald, 2005) and found that loss of lin-12, but not glp-1, phenocopied lag-2 RNAi (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on RNAi experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of sel-12 led to a similar defect in BM gap expansion as lin-29 mutants.
source: Loss of sel-12 led to a similar defect in BM gap expansion as lin-29 mutants (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: The claim is based on genetic analysis shown in Figure 4D,E.

claim: Ablation of the precursors of the π cells on one side of the AC in lin-29(qy1) mutants rescued the BM sliding defect on that side (n = 5/8 animals).
source: To test this notion, we ablated the precursors of the π cells (ventral uterine cells) on one side of the AC in lin-29(qy1) mutants. We found that this treatment rescued the BM sliding defect on that side (n = 5/8 animals, Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is based on laser ablation experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There was little correlation between the timing of π cell divisions and vulE/vulF cell divisions (n = 8/46 π cells in 13 animals dividing coincidently with vulE, n = 16/54 π cells in 12 animals dividing coincidently with vulF).
source: While the π cells began dividing near the same time as the vuE and vulF cells, we found little correlation between the timing of their divisions (n = 8/46 π cells in 13 animals dividing coincidently with vulE on the other side of the BM, n = 16/54 π cells in 12 animals dividing coincidently with vulF on the other side of the BM, Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is based on time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There was no difference in the BM gap size at the P6.p 8-cell stage between animals in which π cell divisions had been arrested compared to wild type controls.
source: We found no difference in the BM gap size at the P6.p 8-cell stage between animals (Hanna-Rose and Han, 1999) in which π cell divisions had been arrested compared to wild type controls (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is based on experiments blocking π cell divisions shown in Figure 5D.

claim: As the BM slid along the π cells to expand the gap, the edge of the BM gap stabilized on the π cells; BM maintained contact with a significant portion the ventral π cells (n = 13/13 animals).
source: In contrast, we found that as the BM slid along the π cells to expand the gap, the edge of the BM gap stabilized on the π cells; BM maintained contact with a significant portion the ventral π cells (n = 13/13 animals imaged during the BM gap expansion, Figure 6A–C).
evidence: The claim is based on imaging data shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: RNAi-mediated knock down of ctg-1 led to a similar BM sliding defect as knock down of the LIN-12/Notch ligand lag-2.
source: Through this screen, we found that RNAi-mediated knock down of ctg-1, which encodes a Sec14-GOLD protein, a poorly understood group of the Sec14 family of phospholipid transfer proteins (Mousley et al., 2007; Saito et al., 2007), led to a similar BM sliding defect as knock down of the LIN-12/Notch ligand lag-2 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is based on RNAi screen data presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Uterine-specific RNAi-mediated knock down of ctg-1 resulted in a BM sliding defect and smaller BM opening.
source: Furthermore, we found that RNAi-mediated knock down of ctg-1 expression in a uterine-specific RNAi strain also resulted in a BM sliding defect and smaller BM opening (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is based on uterine-specific RNAi experiments shown in Figure 7A.

claim: ctg-1 expression is upregulated in the π cells of wild type worms at the time of Notch mediated induction of π cell fate, which coincides with BM sliding.
source: ctg-1 expression is upregulated in the π cells of wild type worms at the time of Notch mediated induction of π cell fate, which coincides with BM sliding (n = >5 animals each stage, top).
evidence: The claim is based on expression analysis using a genomic GFP insertion shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Expression of ctg-1 was not induced when the π cell fate was disrupted in a lin-29 mutant.
source: Expression of ctg-1 was not induced when the π cell fate was disrupted in a lin-29 mutant (n = >5 animals each stage; bottom).
evidence: The claim is based on expression analysis in lin-29 mutants shown in Figure 7B.

claim: A CRISPR-cas9 mediated deletion allele of ctg-1(qy11) has a smaller BM gap compared to wild type.
source: A CRISPR-cas9 mediated deletion allele of ctg-1(qy11) (lateral central plane; DIC, top; laminin::mCherry, bottom) has a smaller BM gap (bracket and arrowheads) compared to a wild type animal.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of a CRISPR-generated mutant shown in Figure 7D,E.

claim: Pan-uterine cell expression of CTG-1 in a lin-29(qy1) mutant increased BM gap size.
source: Pan-uterine cell expression of CTG-1 (fos-1 > ctg-1::GFP) in a lin-29(qy1) mutant increased BM gap size (brackets).
evidence: The claim is based on rescue experiments shown in Figure 7F,G.

claim: The upstream regulatory region of ctg-1 has 19 LAG-1 binding sites.
source: The upstream regulatory region of ctg-1 has 19 LAG-1 binding sites (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), which is why it is predicted to have direct transcriptional regulation by LIN-12/Notch signaling.
evidence: The claim is based on bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reduction of pifk-1 (ortholog of Pik1 and vertebrate PI4KIIIβ), but not other PI4-kinases or ppk-1, decreased BM sliding and gap expansion.
source: In support of a similar role for CTG-1 as Sec14, we found that reduction of pifk-1(ortholog of Pik1 and vertebrate PI4KIIIβ), but not other PI4-kinases or ppk-1, decreased BM sliding and gap expansion (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is based on RNAi experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: There were no changes in the expression or localization of the functional integrin reporter PAT-3::GFP in the lin-29(qy1) mutant background compared to wild type.
source: We did not, however, find any changes in the expression or localization of the functional integrin reporter PAT-3::GFP (Hagedorn et al., 2009) in the lin-29(qy1) mutant background, which lacks ctg-1 expression, compared to wild type (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on imaging analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: FRAP experiments indicated that PAT-3::GFP was trafficked to the cell-BM interface normally at the time of BM sliding in lin-29 mutants.
source: Additionally, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) experiments indicated that PAT-3::GFP was trafficked to the cell-BM interface normally at the time of BM sliding (between P6.p 4-cell and 8-cell stages) in lin-29 mutants (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on FRAP experiments shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: RNAi-mediated targeting of ina-1 in the uterine-specific RNAi background did not rescue BM sliding in lin-29 mutants.
source: Finally, RNAi-mediated targeting of ina-1 in the uterine-specific RNAi background did not rescue BM sliding in lin-29 mutants (BM gap diameter 8.13 ± 0.16 μm (L4440 empty vector control, n = 48), 8.30 ± 0.25 μm [ina-1 RNAi, n = 48]).
evidence: The claim is based on RNAi experiments with quantitative measurements.

claim: There was a significant increase in the localization of DGN-1 at the cell-BM interface in the π cells of lin-29 mutants compared to wild type animals.
source: We detected a significant increase in the localization of DGN-1 at the cell-BM interface in the π cells of lin-29 mutants compared to wild type animals (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: The claim is based on quantitative imaging analysis shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: The transcriptional reporter for dgn-1 was similarly expressed in lin-29 mutants and wild type.
source: This difference was not a result of increased expression, as the transcriptional reporter for dgn-1 was similarly expressed in lin-29 mutants and wild type (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is based on expression analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The localization of DGN-1 in regions beyond the edges of the BM gap (over the vulD cell) were similar in lin-29 and wild type.
source: In addition, the localization of DGN-1 in regions beyond the edges of the BM gap (over the vulD cell) were similar in lin-29 and wild type, indicating that the alteration in DGN-1 localization was specific to the region of BM sliding near the AC (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on imaging analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: FRAP experiments indicated that DGN-1 recovered more quickly after photobleaching in lin-29 mutants versus wild type animals.
source: FRAP experiments indicated that DGN-1 recovered more quickly after photobleaching in lin-29 mutants versus wild type animals, which may account for the increased DGN-1::GFP localization (Figure 8F,G).
evidence: The claim is based on FRAP experiments shown in Figure 8F,G.

claim: The number of DGN-1 containing Rab-7 marked late endosome vesicles in lin-29 mutants and wild type animals was similar.
source: Notably, the number of DGN-1 containing Rab-7 marked late endosome vesicles in lin-29 mutants and wild type animals was similar, suggesting that CTG-1 might not direct rapid removal of DGN-1 from the cell surface into the endosomal system (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is based on co-localization analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: There was a reduction of F-actin at the basal surface in the π cells in lin-29 mutants.
source: There was, however, a reduction of F-actin at the basal surface in the π cells in lin-29 mutants (Figure 8—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is based on F-actin visualization shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 4.

claim: Reduction of dgn-1 expression via uterine specific RNAi in the lin-29(qy1) mutant restored BM sliding and gap expansion.
source: Consistent with this idea, reduction of dgn-1 expression via uterine specific RNAi in the lin-29(qy1) mutant restored BM sliding and gap expansion (Figure 8D,E).
evidence: The claim is based on RNAi rescue experiments shown in Figure 8D,E.

claim: F-actin is thought to act as a barrier to exocytosis.
source: As F-actin is thought to act as a barrier to exocytosis (Eitzen, 2003), these observations support the idea of increased DGN-1 delivery to the cell surface.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Eitzen, 2003).

claim: The GOLD domain and Sec14 proteins are associated with vesicle trafficking.
source: Given the association of the GOLD domain, Sec14 proteins, and PI4-kinase regulation with vesicle trafficking, (Anantharaman and Aravind, 2002; Clayton et al., 2013; Mousley et al., 2007), CTG-1 may direct a specific trafficking pathway that restricts the delivery of DGN-1 to the cell-BM interface.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Anantharaman and Aravind, 2002; Clayton et al., 2013; Mousley et al., 2007).

claim: Sec14 family PITPs are unlikely to be true carriers of phospholipids; instead, they function as scaffolds or nanoreactors that present phosphatidylinositol to phosphatidylinositol-4 kinase (PI4K).
source: Sec14 family PITPs are unlikely to be true carriers of phospholipids. Instead, studies suggest that Sec14 family PITPs function as scaffolds or nanoreactors that present phosphatidylinositol to phosphatidylinositol-4 kinase (PI4K) to regulate specific protein and membrane trafficking pathways in the trans-Golgi and endosomal recycling system (Cockcroft and Garner, 2011; Curwin, 2013; Curwin et al., 2009; Mousley et al., 2008; Schaaf et al., 2008; Tripathi et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The Sec14 family has expanded significantly in multicellular eukaryotes, with yeast having six Sec14 family members, C. elegans having at least 16, and vertebrates having at least 20.
source: The Sec14 family has expanded significantly in multicellular eukaryotes. Whereas yeast have six Sec14 family members, we found C. elegans has at least 16 and vertebrates have at least 20 (Bankaitis et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on bioinformatic analysis and supported by a citation (Bankaitis et al., 2010).

claim: C. elegans make only two integrin heterodimers, and only one of these, αINA-1/βPAT-3, is expressed with DGN-1 (dystroglycan) in the uterine π cells.
source: Unlike mammals, which construct 24 known αβ integrin heterodimers, C. elegans make only two, and only one of these, αINA-1/βPAT-3, is expressed with DGN-1 (dystroglycan) in the uterine π cells (Hagedorn et al., 2009; Ihara et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hagedorn et al., 2009; Ihara et al., 2011).

claim: Dystroglycan is required for branching morphogenesis in glandular epithelium, a process that is thought to require BM sliding.
source: Notably, dystroglycan is also required for branching morphogenesis in glandular epithelium, a process that is thought to require BM sliding (Durbeej et al., 2001; Harunaga et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Durbeej et al., 2001; Harunaga et al., 2014).

claim: Loss of basally localized dystroglycan during chick gastrulation promotes breakdown of BMs during the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition that forms mesoderm.
source: Further, it has been shown that loss of basally localized dystroglycan during chick gastrulation promotes breakdown of BMs during the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition that forms mesoderm (Nakaya et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Nakaya et al., 2011).

claim: Loss or reduction of dystroglycan is emerging as a common event in the progression of epithelial derived cancers, including breast, prostate, colon, cervical, and renal adenocarcinomas.
source: Importantly, loss or reduction of dystroglycan is also emerging as a common event in the progression of epithelial derived cancers, including breast, prostate, colon, cervical, and renal adenocarcinomas (Cross et al., 2008; Esser et al., 2013; Sgambato et al., 2007, 2003, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.
